guide.title: Union Square, Manhattan: Where Protest Meets Produce
guide.intro: Union Square's name marks the union of the island's two principal early thoroughfares, Broadway and the former Bowery Road (now Park Avenue), which meet at the square. Developer Samuel Ruggles convinced the city to enlarge the commons in 1831 and enclose and grade it in 1834; the park opened in July 1839. It quickly became a stage for the nation's biggest moments and movements: on April 20, 1861, after the fall of Fort Sumter, the flag flew from the square's George Washington statue before a rally of perhaps a quarter million people, and on September 5, 1882, at least 10,000 workers paraded past a reviewing stand here in the country's first Labor Day parade — the reason the square was named a National Historic Landmark in 1997. Union Square has stayed a gathering point for labor and radical politics ever since, from Emma Goldman's 1893 speech to the 1934 department store strikes.

sections.heading: A Square Built for Rallies
sections.body: Union Square's Greek Revival design and central location made it New York's default gathering ground almost from the moment it opened in 1839. Henry Kirke Brown's equestrian statue of George Washington, unveiled in 1856, was the first public sculpture erected in the city since the 1770 statue of George III — and it was from that statue that the Fort Sumter flag flew during the quarter-million-person rally of April 1861. The square's radical tradition runs from Emma Goldman's 1893 "Free Bread" speech to the 1934 department store strikes, but its most consequential single day may be September 5, 1882, when at least 10,000 workers marched up Broadway in the country's first Labor Day parade — the achievement the square was designated a National Historic Landmark to honor in 1997. That civic energy still shows up daily at the Union Square Greenmarket, founded in 1976 with seven farmers and now the city's flagship farmers market.

sections.heading: Getting there by subway
sections.body: The 14th Street-Union Square station complex is one of the best-connected spots in the city, served by the 4/5/6 (Lexington Avenue line), the N/Q/R/W (Broadway line), and the L (Canarsie line) — it was the system's fourth-busiest station in 2024, so nearly any Manhattan or Brooklyn destination is a one-seat or one-transfer ride away.

faq.question: How do I get to Union Square by subway?
faq.answer: The 14th Street-Union Square complex puts the 4/5/6, N/Q/R/W, and L trains all at one stop — it was the fourth-busiest station in the entire system in 2024, so most Manhattan and Brooklyn destinations are a one-seat or one-transfer ride away.

faq.question: Where does the name Union Square come from?
faq.answer: It marks the union of Broadway and the former Bowery Road, now Park Avenue north of the square — the island's two principal early thoroughfares, which meet here.

faq.question: What is the Union Square Greenmarket?
faq.answer: Founded in 1976 by the Council on the Environment of New York City (now GrowNYC) with seven original farmers, it now operates Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays, and Saturdays, drawing more than 250,000 customers a week in peak season.

faq.question: Why was Union Square named a National Historic Landmark?
faq.answer: Primarily to honor the first Labor Day parade, held here on September 5, 1882, when at least 10,000 workers marched up Broadway and past a reviewing stand at the square. The designation came in 1997.

faq.question: Where can I stay near Union Square?
faq.answer: The W New York – Union Square, on the northeast corner of the square inside the 1911 Beaux-Arts former Germania Life Insurance Company Building, is the verified in-neighborhood option, following a $100 million renovation completed in 2025.

places.name: Union Square Park
places.address: Bounded by E 14th St (south), E 17th St (north), Union Square West/Broadway and Union Square East/Park Ave S, Manhattan
places.summary: Opened as a public park in July 1839 and named a National Historic Landmark in 1997 as the site of the first Labor Day parade in 1882. Home to Henry Kirke Brown's 1856 equestrian statue of George Washington, the first public sculpture erected in New York City since 1770.

photos.author: Chensiyuan

places.name: Union Square Greenmarket
places.address: North and west plazas of Union Square Park (E 14th-17th Sts), Manhattan
places.summary: Founded in 1976 by the Council on the Environment of NYC (now GrowNYC) with seven farmers; operates Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays, and Saturdays, 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., and serves more than 250,000 customers a week in peak season.

places.name: Strand Book Store
places.address: 828 Broadway (at E 12th St), New York, NY
places.summary: Founded in 1927 and famous for its "18 Miles of Books" slogan — the store now houses more than 23 miles of stock — and called "the undisputed king of the city's independent bookstores" by The New York Times.

places.name: Daryl Roth Theatre
places.address: 101 East 15th Street (at Union Square East), New York, NY
places.summary: An off-Broadway venue occupying the landmark former Union Square Savings Bank, designed by Henry Bacon (architect of the Lincoln Memorial) and built 1905-1907; the complex includes the main theatre (299-499 seats) and the 99-seat DR2 Theatre.

places.name: Union Square Cafe
places.summary: Danny Meyer's flagship restaurant, founded in 1985 and the launching point of his Union Square Hospitality Group; now led by Executive Chef Lena Ciardullo.

places.name: Breads Bakery
places.summary: An Israeli-rooted artisan bakery a block from Union Square Park, known for its chocolate babka, with breads and pastries baked in small batches throughout the day.

places.name: Irving Farm New York
places.summary: A homegrown New York coffee roaster founded in 1996, whose original Irving Place cafe sits two blocks east of Union Square Park.

places.name: W New York – Union Square
places.address: 201 Park Avenue South (50 Union Square East), New York, NY
places.summary: Occupies the Beaux-Arts former Germania Life Insurance Company Building (built 1911) on the northeast corner of Union Square; Marriott purchased the hotel in October 2019, and a $100 million renovation led by designer David Rockwell was completed in 2025.
